title: Nanak and Angad
hookLine: the Ardas remembers Guru Nanak, then Guru Angad

cards: A family business, and the founder is getting old. Everyone assumes the son will take over: that's how it's always done. Then the founder chooses someone else.
Not a relative. A man who came to visit and stayed, who did whatever he was asked, however odd, without arguing. The sons are not pleased.
The town talks. It could be a story about a shop or a farm. Sikhs tell it about the very first handover of the Guruship, and the Ardas, every time it's prayed, says those two names in a row.

teach.h: TURN YOUR MIND TO GURU NANAK.
teach.b: After first remembering the Power, the stanza goes on: guru nanak laeen dhiai, turn your mind to Guru Nanak.

teach.h: LEHNA BECOMES ANGAD: A PART OF ME.
teach.b: Then, phir angad gur te: then to Guru Angad. Guru Nanak needs little introduction by now.
Born in the village now called Nankana Sahib, he traveled widely, sang the hymns that open the Guru Granth Sahib, and settled at Kartarpur, where a community farmed, ate together and sang.
Near the end of his life came the handover. His disciple was a man named Lehna. Sikh tradition tells of tests: tasks that looked pointless or unpleasant, which others refused and Lehna simply did.
Guru Nanak gave him a new name: Angad. Ang means a limb, a part of the body. Tradition hears the name as: you are a part of me.
Guru Nanak had sons, and he passed them over.
The Guruship would go by fitness, not by blood, and Sikhs see that choice as one of the founding moments of the faith. Guru Angad is remembered for quieter things.
Tradition credits him with shaping and spreading the Gurmukhi script, the letters the scripture is written in.

His wife, Mata Khivi, is remembered for running the langar with great generosity; she is named in the Guru Granth Sahib itself, where the bards Satta and Balwand praise her kitchen. And he collected Guru Nanak's hymns.
So when the Ardas says Nanak, then Angad, it isn't just a list. It's the moment a teacher became a lineage, and, as Sikhs say, the same light passed from one person to another.

how: In every Ardas, after Bhagauti, Sikhs remember Guru Nanak and then Guru Angad by name, the first two in the line of ten Gurus.

o: Lehna's new name: you are a part of me
the village where Guru Nanak was born
Guru Nanak's elder son, heir by birth

games.q: Nanak and Angad — tap the pairs.
p: a limb, a part of the body
the script Angad is credited with spreading

s: Guru Nanak passed the Guruship to his son
he passed over his sons and chose his disciple Lehna, renamed Angad.
the name Angad is heard as a part of me
ang means a limb; tradition hears: you are a part of me.
Mata Khivi is praised in the Guru Granth Sahib for her kitchen
the bards Satta and Balwand praise her langar (Ang 967).

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, old now, choosing who will carry the light. your sons are waiting. what does tradition say you do?
o: choose Lehna, the disciple who did every task asked.
games.why: he chose Lehna and named him Angad. Sikhs see the choice of fitness over blood as a founding moment.

practice: On one out-breath, say Nanak, and let a picture come with it: a traveler, a farmer at Kartarpur, a man singing.
On the next, say Angad, and picture someone doing an odd, humble task without complaint; go back and forth, slowly, letting the names become a rhythm.
If you pray, add Waheguru between them; if you don't, think of someone who passed something good on to you.

wordCard.voice: Angad. Guru Nanak's disciple, whom he named a part of himself: the first handover of the Guruship.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Angad, from ang, a limb; the name Guru Nanak gave his disciple Lehna.

carryVoice: Your line: nanak, angad. One light, passed from a teacher to a disciple. See you tomorrow.
